title: Budget by phase, from your own record
outcomes: Turns a time control into seconds for the opening, the middlegame, the endgame and a reserve
Explains why a critical moment, not the phase name, decides where extra clock goes
Reads move numbers off the biggest drops in his own games and tallies them by phase
Writes a phase budget that allows for the opening he actually plays

steps.text: Each phase asks for different thinking. In the opening you mostly recall, until the opponent leaves your preparation. In the middlegame you choose plans. In the endgame a few moves can decide the game. So the shares differ. But **where your critical decisions fall is a fact about your own games**: read it from the record, not from a guess.

steps.prompt: Time control 10+5 and 40 moves: 600 seconds plus 40 × 5 is 800 seconds in all. Try this split: reserve 10%, opening 15%, middlegame 55%, endgame 20%. Work out the seconds before you read on.

steps.text: **Mark the boundaries from the record.** Rules of thumb to try: the opening ends at the first move you did not know from your preparation; the endgame starts when queens are off or few pieces remain. Your own opening matters: a line you know costs little until the opponent leaves it, a sharp line can need clock early. A critical decision can fall in any phase.

steps.caption: White to move, move 10. The h3 pawn can take the bishop on g4. This is the opening, and already a critical moment.

line.say: hxg4 takes the bishop on g4. It looks like a free piece.
Qxh1+ takes the rook on h1 with check: the h-file is open.
Bf1 blocks the check. White has given a rook for a bishop.
Nxg4 takes the pawn as well.

claims.statement: hxg4 is rated at least four pawns worse than the best move.
Along the engine line hxg4 ends with White three or more points down.
O-O, Qd2 and Nc3 are the engine's top moves, within 40 centipawns of each other.

steps.title: Which position needs the extra?
steps.prompt: The first position was from move 8 and the usual share was enough. This one is from move 19: does it need extra clock (critical) or the usual share (routine)? Predict, then check. The stage alone does not decide it: the move 10 board you saw earlier was critical too.

steps.text: **No record, no phase budget.** A **drop** is a move after which the engine's score for you fell by a pawn or more. Count where yours fell, using first-guess boundaries: moves 1 to 12, 13 to 30, 31 on. Test moving extra clock to the phase with most drops; recheck after ten games. A tactic in the first ten moves needs the safety scan and a look at the reply.

steps.prompt: An invented example, not data. One player's ten biggest drops in five games happened at moves 6, 9, 14, 17, 18, 22, 23, 27, 33 and 41. Count them by phase: moves 1 to 12, 13 to 30, and 31 on. The middlegame spans 18 moves and the opening 12, so compare counts with care.

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** After you run the engine on a game, *My games* lists up to five of your biggest drops with move numbers; tally them by hand. The analysis is quick, so one drop is a lead. The app does not sort drops by phase or record your clock. After ten tallied games you can revise the shares without this page.

steps.prompt: Use the biggest drops from your analysed games. If you have none yet, leave the counts at zero and treat the shares as a guess to revise.

fields.label: The opening I play, for the clock:
options: I know my lines well: a smaller opening share
my opening is sharp or new to me: a larger opening share
